sections.body: Citation mapping and discovery is the study of how research papers connect through references and shared meaning. In practice, artificial intelligence reads the text and reference lists of papers, builds a graph of which papers cite which, and groups papers by similar claims or methods. It also tracks how a single paper is cited over time, whether as background, method, or challenge. The goal is to help a researcher see a field as a network rather than a list of search results.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The work is useful for small, well defined collections, but it is not a solved problem. The site's library of 135 research papers and 10,555 extracted claims is large enough to show local patterns, such as which papers cluster together or which older paper is suddenly being cited more. However, citation counts and similarity scores can miss important differences, and a paper may be cited to disagree with it, not to support it. Honest limits include messy metadata, paywalled full text, and the fact that a citation graph only shows formal references, not informal influence.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: Citation Graphs Over Time shows how a paper's incoming links rise, fall, or shift in purpose, while How a Paper Is Cited looks at the sentence level to separate support from criticism. Clustering Papers by Meaning groups papers by what they actually claim, not just by shared references, which helps when two fields use different words for the same idea. Bridge Studies Between Fields identifies papers that connect otherwise separate clusters, and Forecasting Research Trends uses those connections to suggest where attention may move next. A reader would start with the first two pages to understand the raw structure, then use the clustering and bridge pages to find related work, and turn to the forecasting page only after seeing how fragile the underlying signals are.
